First, we recall the definition of an injection:

A function $f:X\to Y$ is an injection if every element $x\in X$ is mapped to a distinct element in $Y:$

$$
{x}_{1}\ne {x}_{2}\,⇒\,f({x}_{1})\ne f({x}_{2})
$$

In this case, it would be easier to prove the contrapositive statement. 

This implication is equivalent to its contrapositive:

$$
f({x}_{1})=f({x}_{2})\,⇒\,{x}_{1}={x}_{2}
$$

Now, we simply need to derive ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}$ by assuming that $f({x}_{1})=f({x}_{2}),$ where ${x}_{1}=({z}_{1},{w}_{1})$ and ${x}_{2}=({z}_{2},{w}_{2}):$

So, let $({z}_{1},{w}_{1}),({z}_{2},{w}_{2})\in C\times C,$ and suppose that $f({z}_{1},{w}_{1})=f({z}_{2},{w}_{2}).$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({z}_{1},{w}_{1}) & =f({z}_{2},{w}_{2}) \\ (\overset{―}{{z}_{1}-{w}_{1}},{z}_{1}\text{i}+{w}_{1}) & =(\overset{―}{{z}_{2}-{w}_{2}},{z}_{2}\text{i}+{w}_{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Since two pairs are equal if and only if their respective components are equal, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{{z}_{1}-{w}_{1}}=\overset{―}{{z}_{2}-{w}_{2}} \\ {z}_{1}\text{i}+{w}_{1}={z}_{2}\text{i}+{w}_{2}\end{aligned} & \,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}-{w}_{1}={z}_{2}-{w}_{2} \\ {z}_{1}\text{i}+{w}_{1}={z}_{2}\text{i}+{w}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & \,⇒\,{z}_{1}+{z}_{1}\text{i}={z}_{2}+{z}_{2}\text{i} \\  & \,⇒\,{z}_{1}(1+\text{i})={z}_{2}(1+\text{i}) \\  & \,⇒\,{z}_{1}={z}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}\text{i}+{w}_{1} & ={z}_{1}\text{i}+{w}_{2} \\ {w}_{1} & ={w}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we state the conclusion:

Hence, $({z}_{1},{w}_{1})=({z}_{2},{w}_{2}),$ as was to be shown. Therefore, $f$ is an injection.
